Sometimes, mystified by the behaviorof one of my sons, my wife will point out if it’s age-appropriate, making me wonder why I still shout at ballplayers on tv and argue with the dead. Last week, my oldest son,with a wild pitch, turned my left ankle into an eggplant. I didn’t yell at the doctors who refused my insurance, or get angry with a friend who told me to soak it in bourbon and garlic. No,I read Montaigne who said self-revelation is the purpose of discourse, which, in his day, meant knowing whether to be flattered if a friend didn’t use a food-taster, or amused if a witch cast a spell of weeping on an in-law. Blaise Monluc, the king’s lieutenant general during the civil wars, Montaigne says,threw so many hanged Protestantsdown a well you could reach in and touch the top one’s head. Yes,Monluc, who was fond of saying “When the scaffolds are full, use trees,” knew what was appropriate. On occasion I’ll run into a lobbyto avoid greeting a friend, not because my mind vanishes and I can’t remember his name, which is true, but because I must flee what is darkest in me. In other words, when evicted from a strange lobby into a stranger street, where every scaffold is full and bodies dangle in the long blue sorrow of the afternoon, without context, explanation, or sympathy,it’s good to know, even momentarily, how to live, among the relevant, the passionate, and the confused.

Whenever my spouse reassures me that our son’s odd conduct is merely a typical phase of childhood development, it prompts me to question my own maturity—particularly why I continue to scream at athletes on the television screen and engage in mental debates with the deceased. A few days ago, my firstborn’s errant throw left my left ankle swollen and severely discolored. Despite the pain, I didn't lose my temper with the medical staff who rejected my health coverage, nor did I get upset with a companion who advised me to soak the injury in a concoction of garlic and spirits. 

Rather than reacting in anger, I turned to the works of Montaigne, who maintained that the true aim of conversation is to reveal one's inner soul. In his time, this required navigating unique social realities, such as knowing to feel honored if a host dined with you without a food-taster present, or being amused when a sorcerer afflicted an in-law with constant weeping. Montaigne also described Blaise Monluc, a royal commander during French religious conflicts, who dumped so many executed Protestants down a water well that you could stretch out a hand and graze the head of the uppermost body. Indeed, Monluc—who famously declared that trees should serve as gallows once the official scaffolds were full—had his own brutal concept of proper conduct.

Occasionally, I will slip into an unfamiliar building entryway just to avoid greeting an acquaintance. This isn't merely because my memory fails me and I forget their name—though that frequently happens—but because I feel an urgent need to escape the darkest corners of my own psyche. Ultimately, when forced out of a quiet refuge back onto an indifferent street—where every gallows is occupied, bodies swing beneath a gloomy afternoon sky, and no meaning, reason, or pity is offered—there is value in discovering, if only for a fleeting moment, how to exist alongside those who are meaningful, intense, and profoundly confused.

Here is a complete, well-structured essay expanded from your bullet points:

***

We spend much of our lives operating under the silent assumption that adulthood brings with it a natural, steadying wisdom. We expect that as the years accumulate, our behavior will automatically align with some invisible standard of maturity. Yet, I often find myself contemplating what it truly means to act “age-appropriately,” forced to confront the embarrassing reality of my own lingering, irrational habits. Despite the graying at my temples and the weight of my responsibilities, I am frequently unsettled by how easily childish pettiness, unwarranted anxiety, and strange, instinctual defense mechanisms can still govern my actions.

This gap between expected maturity and actual human frailty became starkly clear to me recently following a household accident. A moment of chaotic play ended with my young son unintentionally causing me a painful injury. In the immediate aftermath—amidst the sterile tension of medical waiting rooms, the mild incompetence of overworked doctors, and the well-meaning but ultimately useless platitudes of friends—an old, destructive rage flared inside me. It would have been easy to lash out, to externalize my physical discomfort as anger toward everyone around me. Instead, I chose a different path of retreat: I reached for philosophy. 

I immersed myself in the *Essays* of Michel de Montaigne, seeking a quiet sanctuary from my irritation. Reading Montaigne, one is immediately struck by his obsession with human nature and the shifting definitions of decorum across history. He observed how societies rigidly enforce arbitrary standards of social appropriateness, often while indulging in or turning a blind eye to immense, brutal violence. Montaigne mapped out a world where historical figures were celebrated for their refined manners even as they ordered atrocities. This stark contrast between surface-level propriety and underlying barbarism served as a sobering mirror, forcing me to question the very nature of my own frustration.

More importantly, it compelled me to acknowledge the darker, more volatile impulses within myself. I am not immune to the contradictions Montaigne documented. I recognize in my own chest a quiet, dark turbulence—an irrational urge to burn bridges, to isolate myself, or to engage in erratic, avoidant behavior around the people I care about most. There are moments when the pressure of social expectations becomes too much, and my instinct is not to communicate, but to disappear, alienating friends with sudden withdrawals and unprovoked coldness.

Ultimately, reading philosophy through the fog of physical pain and personal irritation offered no simple cures, but it provided something far more valuable: perspective. True maturity, I realized, does not mean achieving a state of flawless, enlightened calm, nor does it mean pretending our darkest impulses do not exist. Rather, it lies in the ongoing effort to understand ourselves. In a world that is so often grim, chaotic, and fundamentally confusing, the highest goal we can strive for is simply learning how to exist within it meaningfully—navigating our own imperfections with grace, patience, and a bit of honest self-reflection.
outputs.L4:
There are moments in an adult life when the mask of maturity slips, leaving behind a jarring self-portrait of pettiness, overreaction, and childish grace: a sudden outburst over a misplaced key, an unreasonable flare of jealousy, or a stubborn refusal to concede a trivial argument. We are taught that aging brings a natural, linear progression toward wisdom and emotional equilibrium. Yet, when faced with my own recurring, irrational reactions, I find myself questioning what “age-appropriate behavior” truly means. Are we ever fully rational, or do we merely learn to cover our volatile impulses with a polished veneer? 

To make sense of these personal mishaps, I turned to the sixteenth-century philosopher Michel de Montaigne, a thinker who turned self-scrutiny into an art form. Retiring to his tower library amidst the madness of his era, Montaigne did not write to present himself as a stoic ideal. Instead, he painted himself in all his contradictions—confessing to his poor memory, his physical anxieties, his fickle moods, and his intellectual limitations. Montaigne recognized that human beings are fundamentally inconsistent creatures, governed far more by custom, emotion, and bodily whims than by pure reason. By exposing his own flaws so nakedly, he offered a quiet reassurance: to be irrational is not a failure of character, but an inherent condition of being human.

Yet Montaigne’s project of self-revelation was not conducted in a vacuum. Outside his tower walls, France was being torn apart by the Wars of Religion—a period of horrifying civil strife characterized by unimaginable brutality, fanaticism, and neighbor turning against neighbor. As Montaigne recorded the atrocities of his time, he observed how quickly abstract dogmas could curdle into senseless violence. The madness of the individual, when multiplied across a culture, birthed a collective slaughter that defied all logic. Reading his accounts, one realizes that the grand theater of human history is driven by the exact same dark, inexplicable absurdities that govern our smallest personal errors. The petty ego that sparks a domestic quarrel is the same untamed spark that, under different conditions, ignites a war.

Through this lens, the illusion of a neat, orderly world dissolves. History is not a steady march toward enlightenment, nor is personal life a smooth ascent into flawless adulthood. Both are bound to a tangled web of passion, error, and inexplicable chaos. We are, by nature, flawed actors navigating an unpredictable stage.

Ultimately, this realization does not demand despair; rather, it offers a profound form of liberation. If human history and individual nature are irrevocably messy, the goal of life cannot be the total eradication of our irrationality. Instead, the true challenge lies in the delicate, vital art of learning how to live. It is the practice of carving out brief moments of clarity, grace, and humor amidst the world’s passionate and confused reality. To accept our shared absurdity is not to surrender to it, but to find a way to navigate the noise—discovering, if only for a fleeting moment, how to exist peacefully with ourselves and one another in all our flawed complexity.
outputs.L5:
Human nature resists static definitions. We prefer to imagine ourselves as monuments carved from granite—steadfast, predictable, and clear—yet we are far more like shadows cast by windblown branches. **Montaigne** understood this truth better than most. Retreating to the quiet solitude of his tower library in 16th-century France, surrounded by Latin maxims painted on the ceiling beams, he set out to record the most unpredictable subject he could find: himself.

In doing so, Montaigne pioneered a revolutionary form of writing—the essay—which at its core is a record of human inconsistency. **Sometimes**, we awake feeling capable of moving mountains, convinced of our own wisdom and purpose. At other times, the smallest setback reduces us to doubt and fatigue. A single afternoon can host a dozen conflicting versions of who we are. To deny this variability is to do violence to the reality of the human condition. **Sometimes**, as Montaigne famously observed, the only thing certain about our behavior is its uncertainty. 

This constant ebb and flow naturally makes us ponder what will **last**. In a world where emotions fade, opinions shift, and bodies age, what endures? Montaigne’s answer was not to construct grand, rigid philosophical systems designed to outlive the stars. Instead, he suggested that what truly **last**s is our capacity for honest self-examination and acceptance. He wrote openly about his fears, his digestive troubles, his loves, and his dread of dying, proving that vulnerability outlives pretense.

We often live as though our current state of mind is permanent, forgetting that every season passes and every thought must eventually yield to the next. Every breath we take brings us closer to our **last**, yet this impermanence is not a tragedy—it is what gives weight to the present. **Sometimes**, the quietest moments of reflection, spent honestly confronting our own flaws and fleeting joys, are the ones that leave the deepest mark. In the end, to live fully is to embrace the "sometimes" of our daily shifts while preparing gracefully for the **last**, learning, as Montaigne did, to be at home within our own restless minds.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a reflective prose poem about middle age, fatherhood, and moral self-awareness. Include a detail about a minor injury caused by a son, a reference to Montaigne's essays (specifically citing Blaise Monluc), and a moment of fleeing a building lobby to avoid an acquaintance.
counterfactuals.output:
The middle of life is a house where the doors have begun to swell in their frames; nothing shuts quite as smoothly as it used to, and every draft carries the scent of turning leaves. This morning, my five-year-old son misjudged the arc of his wild, morning leap, the hard crown of his skull colliding with my jaw and splitting my lip against my own incisors. The blood was bright, sudden, and hot, a vivid drop of mortality spilled on the kitchen tile by the very life I am tasked with keeping safe. As I pressed a cold towel to my mouth, he wept for my pain—a brief, sweet inversion where the child seeks absolution from the bruised altar of his father’s face, unaware that the sting was less from the blow than from the swift, terrifying realization of how easily we are broken by the things we love.

I wear the swelling now like a minor badge of authority, though authority feels increasingly like a costume that no longer fits. It makes me think of Montaigne sitting in his stone tower, writing of the old soldier Blaise de Monluc, who spent his final days drowned in a bitter, inconsolable grief. Monluc had lost his son in the wars, but his true torment was moral: he had maintained a grim, martial distance throughout the boy's life, hiding his deep affection behind a mask of stern discipline, leaving the youth to die without ever knowing how fiercely his father had adored him. To hold back love out of some foolish allegiance to dignity—is there a more pathetic form of cowardice?

And yet, how fluently I practice my own small cowardices, unembellished by the tragic gravity of a French marshal. Just an hour ago, stepping into the high, echoing marble of the office lobby, I caught sight of an acquaintance by the elevators—a man whose quiet demands for small talk required a currency of spirit I simply did not possess. Before his eyes could meet mine, I turned sharply on my heel, slipping back through the glass revolving doors and into the grey drizzle of the street, pretending to search for something in my coat pocket. I hid in the cold air, a middle-aged man fleeing a ghost of his own social obligation, terrified of being seen in his exhaustion.

I am a father who winces when his child jumps, a man who ducks behind the city’s revolving doors to preserve a thin margin of peace, caught somewhere between the stern, regretful ghost of Monluc and the reckless tenderness of the nursery. I touch the split skin of my lip with the tip of my tongue. The metallic taste remains. It stings, but it is a good sting—a sharp, necessary reminder that to be bruised by a child’s love is a grace, and that the only true disaster is to reach the end of the corridor with a heart still perfectly intact, uninjured, and entirely unspent.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a dark, humorous prose poem exploring the concept of "age-appropriate" behavior.
counterfactuals.output: At twenty-two, society permits you to vomit into a potted fern, provided you wear vintage velvet while doing so and refer to the incident as "finding yourself." By thirty-five, however, the fern is an insult to the room’s minimalist aesthetic; you must instead funnel your bile into a spreadsheet and obsess over the structural integrity of your kitchen counters. There is a precise, invisible ledger that dictates when you must stop dancing like a wounded insect and start eyeing lawnmowers with a quiet, erotic reverence. At forty, it is entirely age-appropriate to harbor a deep, sensual hatred for ambient noise, and to spend twenty minutes explaining the nuance of your lumbar spine to a cashier who only asked if you found everything alright. To act twenty at fifty is a grotesque tragedy, but to act eighty at forty—to sit on a porch, chewing softened bran, watching the sky with the grim satisfaction of a beast waiting for the slaughterhouse truck—that is considered maturity. We learn to refine our horror. We trade the visceral thrill of screaming into the night for the dignified pleasure of complaining about a draft. By seventy, the only truly age-appropriate behavior is to slowly dissolve into a cloud of talcum powder and mild hostility, staring straight through your grandchildren until they realize you aren't looking at them at all, but rather at the exact date of their ultimate demise, printed neatly across their unwrinkled foreheads.

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you draft a literary piece that weaves together a mundane domestic anecdote—like getting hit by a bad pitch—with brutal historical references from the French Wars of Religion to meditate on the absurdity of modern human existence?
counterfactuals.output:
The ball—a high-density core of cork and rubber wrapped in synthetic yellow leather—left the pitcher’s hand with a dull, wet snap. 

The pitcher was Todd, a senior logistics coordinator who wore compression sleeves on his knees and took his turn in the Tuesday night co-ed rec league with the grim, joyless intensity of a man trying to outrun a failing marriage. The pitch was inside. Extremely inside. It was an errant, parabolic catastrophe of a throw, humming through the muggy June air at perhaps forty-five miles per hour.

I did not move. Whether through frozen reflex or a subconscious, nihilistic desire to earn a walk, I simply stood in the batter’s box, bathed in the hum of halogen floodlights, and let the sphere strike me squarely in the soft, unarmored meat above my right hip.

*Thwack.*

It was a sound like a wet sack of flour hitting a linoleum floor. The air evacuated my lungs in a sharp, embarrassing wheeze. Pain, sudden and blooming, radiated outward from the point of impact, instantly purple-stippling the capillaries beneath my skin. I doubled over, hands on my knees, staring into the trampled dirt behind home plate. 

"Take your base, man!" shouted the umpire, a teenager chewing rhythmically on a gas-station slim jim. "You okay?"

I nodded, unable to speak, clutching my side. And as I shuffled toward first base, my boots heavy in the manicured dust, the localized trauma of my bruised oblique collapsed the centuries. My mind, reeling from a completely harmless, entirely voluntary physical agony, leapt backward across four hundred and fifty years to the muddy streets of Paris.

Pain, I realized, is a terribly unoriginal sensation. 

I thought of August 24, 1572. The Feast of Saint Bartholomew. 

There, under a sky far darker than this floodlit suburban park, the church bells of Saint-Germain-l'Auxerrois tolled not to mark the end of an inning, but to signal the start of a butcher’s harvest. Duke Henri de Guise’s men broke down the door of Admiral Gaspard de Coligny, a man who had committed the unpardonable sin of believing the body of Christ was symbolically, rather than physically, present in a piece of bread. They stabbed Coligny in his bed, tossed his bleeding, still-breathing frame out of a high window into the courtyard, defiled his corpse, and dragged his headless torso through the gutter to hang by its feet at the gallows of Montfaucon.

Over the next three days, ten thousand Huguenots were butchered across France. Pregnant women were thrown into the Seine; children had their brains dashed against cobblestones; street urchins played with severed ears. In Paris, neighbors killed neighbors over the precise mechanics of grace, over whether a priest’s Latin possessed the magical chemistry to turn cheap wine into God’s literal blood. They waded through knee-deep gore, convinced that the universe hung in the balance of their savagery, that the divine eye was fixed intently on the purity of their hatred.

Now, in the Year of Our Lord 2024, I was hobbling to first base because Todd from logistics had let a soft-stitch ball slip from his sweaty palm. 

I stood on the canvas bag, resting my hands on my hips, feeling the hematoma swell against the waistband of my $35 polyester shorts. Around me, the world hummed in its tranquil, post-historical emptiness. 

Behind the chain-link fence, someone’s golden retriever barked at a passing Honda Civic. A child spilled an ICEE on her crocs. On the adjacent field, "The Base-ic Pitches" were cheering because a middle-aged real estate agent had managed to lay down a successful bunt. 

The absurdity of it crushed down heavier than the pain in my side. 

For millennia, human beings inflicted and endured catastrophic bodily ruin in the name of cosmic certainty. During the Siege of Sancerre in 1573, surrounded by Catholic forces, the starving Protestant townspeople ate boiled leather belts, crushed slate, fried dung, and eventually, in absolute despair, dug up the dead to grind their bones into meal. They suffered the unspeakable because they believed their suffering meant something—that it was recorded in a great golden ledger in the sky, that their agony was a brutal currency traded for eternal salvation.

We conquered that madness. We tamed the religious wars. We built a secular, sanitized world of strip malls, air conditioning, HR departments, and suburban parks. We traded the stake and the rack for safety and comfort. 

And yet, lacking the high drama of salvation and damnation, we invented this. 

Here we were, a collection of accountants, dental hygienists, and software developers, voluntarily gathering on a Tuesday evening to recreate the physical anxiety of combat in miniature. We pay league fees for the privilege of putting our aging joints, our hamstrings, and our soft tissues in harm's way, all to chase a plastic trophy sponsored by a local HVAC repair company. We seek out minor, controlled suffering—bruises, sprains, torn ACLs—because a life entirely devoid of friction feels unnervingly like nonexistence.

"Lead off, buddy! Watch the pickoff!" yelled our third-base coach, Dave, a man who wore a GPS watch to track his heart rate while standing entirely still.

"Right," I muttered to myself. 

I took a two-step lead off the bag. The bruise on my side throbbed in time with my pulse, a sharp, stupid reminder that I was made of meat and nerves. 

Across the diamond, Todd gripped the ball, staring in at the batter with a look of fierce, desperate concentration, as if the fate of his immortal soul depended on the next pitch. I looked up past the glow of the stadium lights, into the vast, indifferent blackness of the night sky, where no angels watched and no ledgers were kept. 

The pitch was delivered. The batter swung. The ball flew harmlessly into the night air, high above the manicured grass, and for a brief, glorious second, we all looked up, pretending it mattered.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem in the style of contemporary reflective American poetry about an aging father coping with physical pain, social anxiety, and his own dark impulses while reading classical essays.
counterfactuals.output:
The L4 vertebra is a dry twig ready to snap 
every time I shift in the leather armchair. 
It is four in the afternoon, the light on the rug 
the pale, exhausted yellow of old bone. 

Across the street, Mrs. Gable prunes her hydrangeas. 
I pull the blinds down another inch so she won’t see me watching, 
so she won’t wave. If she waves, I must go out onto the porch, 
and the porch means the crushing machinery of small talk: 
*How is the weather? How are the knees?* 
My heart knocks against my ribs like a trapped sparrow—
the simple, humiliating panic of being perceived.

Instead, I open Montaigne. 
*That to Philosophize is to Learn to Die.* 
He wrote it in his quiet tower while the plague took the valley, 
his own body burdened with gravel and stone, 
yet he writes of his decay as if it were a polite guest 
he has agreed to sit with until morning. 
In the margin, I find a note I wrote in blue ink thirty years ago: 
*Wisdom is the mastery of the irrational.* 
What an arrogant, healthy young man I was. 

Sciatica fires down my left leg, a white wire of heat. 
And with the burning comes the old shadow, 
the dark dog that trots beside the walker. 
I look at the heavy brass paperweight on the end table 
and feel the sudden, electric urge to throw it through the window—
to hear the sudden, violent music of glass breaking, 
to shock the quiet street into awareness. 
Or the impulse, darker still, that came yesterday 
when my daughter brought the boys over: 
a cold, sudden flash as my grandson ran toward the stairs—
*what if I didn't reach out? What if I just watched him fall?*

The intrusive thoughts are like starlings now; 
they roost in the rafters of an aging mind. 
Pain makes a landlord out of malice.

Seneca says the wise man is self-sufficient, 
that fear is merely a failure of perspective. 
I close the book. The spine is cracked, the cloth cover frayed. 
My daughter will call at six. 
I will put on the smooth, gentle voice of a grandfather, 
the one I keep in the drawer with the reading glasses 
and the prescription bottles. 
I will tell her the garden is coming along. 
I will not tell her about the window, or the mailman’s shadow 
that sent me retreating into the dark hallway like a moth.

I sit still and wait for the bad thought to cool. 
I shift my weight. The lower back clicks—a small, submissive prayer. 
The essay lies open on my lap, 
four hundred years of elegant, stoic endurance 
resting on knees that no longer know how to kneel.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Give me a prose poem that starts with a wife commenting on age-appropriateness and ends with a meditation on how to live among "the relevant, the passionate, and the confused," referencing Michel de Montaigne along the way.
counterfactuals.output:
“That jacket isn’t really age-appropriate anymore,” she says, not unkindly, pointing her tea spoon at the faded crimson leather hanging by the door—a relic from a decade when I still believed intensity was a suitable substitute for style. I look at the sleeves, creased with the ghost of arms that used to gesture wildly at midnight, and wonder at what exact age we are supposed to exchange our bright, foolish skins for the muted wools of resignation. It is the quiet tax of time, this demand for dignity, as if growing old were a court trial where we must plead guilty to our years and dress accordingly. 

But Michel de Montaigne spent his fifties in a high round room surrounded by a thousand books and his own failing kidneys, writing not to polish a legacy, but to measure the exact, humiliating temperature of his own contradictions. He knew that the highest wisdom is merely the willingness to admit we are all fumbling in oversized robes, and that even on the loftiest throne in Christendom, a man is still sitting only on his own hindquarters. He did not ask if his desires were age-appropriate; he asked only if his mind was nimble enough to catch itself in the act of being absurd. 

Outside our window, the street hums with the electric noise of the evening. The young drift down the sidewalk in glossy clusters, their laughter sharp and uncalibrated, carrying their bright, fragile convictions like lit matches in a dry wind. It would be so easy to pull the curtains, to sit in the soft, sensible lamplight and pretend I have solved the riddle of the world simply by outliving my own impulses. But Montaigne’s ghost taps his silver quill against my knuckle, reminding me that to retreat from the noise is to die before the pulse stops. The real work, the late-life work, is not to put on the gray armor of the spectator, but to figure out how to stand in the doorway—slightly out of step, fully aware of the absurdity of my own red leather—learning at last how to live gracefully among the relevant, the passionate, and the confused.
